items.original_title: How close is shipping to the top?
items.summary: Shipping markets rarely announce the top with any clarity. More often, the argument about whether the peak has arrived only really starts when freight rates are still climbing, asset values are making less and less conventional sense and owners are sufficiently confident to keep buying ships at prices that would have looked ridiculous a few months earlier. Chief correspondent Adis Adjin assesses where we are in today’s record high shipping cycle. But there are enough signs beneath the surface to start asking a more awkward question: how much of this cycle is left, and which sectors are closest to finding out? The comparison with the last supercycle has its limits — today’s orderbook is equivalent to around 23% of the fleet, against more than 50% at the 2008 peak — but the direction of travel is clear. The bigger issue is what happens to the amount of large tonnage still scheduled to emerge from Asian yards, much of it above 12,000 teu, while a large share of the chartered fleet that can be returned sits below 8,000 teu. Central to the programme are six new quay cranes and 16 rubber-tyred gantry cranes, forming part of the port’s wider USD 108 million investment in container-handling machinery and supporting assets. “The one-million-TEU milestone shows that HIP’s container business is moving into a new stage of growth. items.title: Strong Freight Markets Keep Aging Ships Out of Recycling Yards
items.original_title: Strong Freight Markets Keep Aging Ships Out of Recycling Yards
items.summary: Strong freight markets kept aging vessels trading through the third quarter despite rising scrap prices and strong demand from ship recyclers, according to a new market review from GMS, the world’s largest cash buyer of ships for recycling. The ship recycling market entered the quarter looking ripe for an increase in demolition activity. GMS said it was tracking roughly 550 merchant vessels preparing to exit the Gulf at the start of July, including around 200 bulk carriers, while recycling yards in the major South Asian markets had available capacity and appetite for tonnage. The report argues that owners were weighing recycling offers against a much broader set of alternatives, including freight earnings, secondhand sale opportunities, remaining vessel life, route risks and compliance costs. GMS expects recycling supply to remain tight into the fourth quarter as long as vessel earnings remain strong, particularly where ships continue to find lucrative employment linked to the Strait of Hormuz. But those delayed recycling decisions may be creating a larger pool of aging tonnage that will eventually need to leave the fleet. If freight earnings normalize, secondhand liquidity weakens or employment opportunities narrow, GMS said some of that deferred supply could reach recycling markets over a much shorter period.

items.title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.original_title: South Korea-Russia ocean volumes boosted by rail congestion in China
items.summary: Growing congestion along the Trans-China and Trans-Siberian railways, linking China and Russia, has boosted South Korea-Russia container volumes, encouraging shipping lines to consider deploying larger vessels this month. In August, more than 33,000 teu was transported from Busan to ports in Russia’s far east, such as Vladivostok, a slight increase on July. Of this, exports, excluding transhipment cargo, were 8,000 teu. Volumes are said to have remained at the same level in September, as South Korean shippers rushed to get cargo out before the country’s Thanksgiving Day holiday on 25-26 September and China’s week-long National Day on 1 October. Consequently, cargo “rollovers”, where shipments are delayed due to a lack of space, are becoming increasingly frequent and Busan-Vladivostok freight rates now average $1,700 per teu, up from $1,500 per teu in August, which had seen a $300 jump from July. A representative at Dong Young Shipping, which offers South Korea-Russia services, said: “We’re considering deploying larger vessels than those currently in use, so we can offer more slots.” Congestion around major Chinese hub ports following the East Asia typhoon season in August resulted in more Chinese shippers opting for rail freight to Europe. And as rail capacity has failed to keep pace with the surge in cargo volume, waiting times for train departures now exceed one week.

items.original_title: Empty box pile-up at port of Manila sparks truckers’ strike
items.summary: Customs brokers and hauliers are expected to voluntarily stop work today in advance of a three-day trucking strike in Manila, as a year-long standoff on carriers failing to remove their empties reaches its limit – Hapag-Lloyd having suspended bookings amid the chaos. Warning the protest could “last a week”, Reynaldo Soliman, chair of the Practicing Customs Brokers and Port Truckers Alliance, urged brokers not to secure gate passes, book trucks, or release shipments, until carriers reduced the number of empties at Manila. “Even though we want to ship, we cannot move,” Mr Soliman told local reporters, with the number of empties scattered around terminals, hauliers yards, and waiting on flatbeds to be removed, measured in the thousands with just 10% of volumes moving out of Manila’s ports. In a letter seen by The Loadstar , Bureau of Customs commissioner Ariel Nepomuceno told Port of Manila it needed to take measures to address the worsening empties backlog, suggesting boxes that had been waiting for more than 10 days be moved offsite. “Increasing yard utilisation levels at the Manila International Container Port and the port of Manila continue to adversely affect the efficient movement of cargo and the overall flow of port operations,” he wrote.

items.title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.original_title: South Africa’s port reform takes an important step forward
items.summary: One battle doesn’t win a war, but just getting to a stage where South Africa’s port system can now be reformed is an achievement by itself. The decision of South Africa’s government to formally endorse the separation of Transnet National Port Authority (TNPA), the country’s de facto port landlord, from the Transnet rail operations is a step in the right direction – one that its shippers, forwarders, and other supply chain stakeholders have been demanding for years. Operations at South Africa’s key container gateways of Durban, Cape Town, Coega and Port Elizabeth have been plagued by congestion and delays for years. And while it’s great the government has finally kicked off the reform process of Transnet, it also means some of the really hard work begins now, as the South African Association of Freight Forwarders argues when it says the real imperative is “getting corporatisation right”. The central point of the reform is that TNPA will be moved out of the Transnet group – which will continue to manage Transnet Port Terminals, but with much reduced investment power – and become a standalone state organisation with the ability to take its own investment decisions on both infrastructure and superstructure, and independently manage landlord revenues.

In 2025, the EU steel industry consumed 74.4 million mt of ferrous scrap. Its H1 2026 intake of 38.1 million mt has kept EU steel production and ferrous scrap utilization broadly in line with the first half of 2025, but Europe’s accelerating transition toward more electric steelmaking will trigger a surge in the EU’s steel scrap demand, according to Eurofer. items.summary: Japan has imposed sanctions directly on individual vessels for the first time, targeting 35 ships linked to Russia’s shadow fleet as Tokyo steps up efforts to restrict Moscow’s oil-export network. The measures took effect on October 2 under Japan’s Foreign Exchange and Foreign Trade Act. Japanese companies will now need government permission to provide specified services to the 35 vessels and for capital transactions, including loans and debt guarantees, connected with their sale, purchase, lease or charter. Japan’s foreign ministry has identified all 35 ships by IMO number. It is the first time Tokyo has placed vessels themselves under sanctions, bringing Japan closer to the approach already adopted by the UK and European Union against ageing tankers moving Russian oil outside mainstream Western shipping, finance and insurance channels. The shipping measures formed part of a wider package that also froze the assets of 33 Russian organisations and nine individuals and introduced export restrictions against four entities in Turkey and the UAE. Tokyo said the vessel measures were aimed at ships being used to transport Russian crude and petroleum products while circumventing existing sanctions. items.title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.original_title: Where freight forwarders actually lose money
items.summary: More often than not, a forwarder closes a clean month and still watches the margins come in light. Most forwarders already know where it went: into the charges that were never recovered and the costs that were never meant to happen. A demurrage charge that was never passed on to the customer. Forwarders already have more data than they can read. Everything after is just a record of money already gone. So, the job is narrower than what most tech pitches: flag the handful of shipments where an unexpected charge is about to be incurred, whether that is demurrage building, a customs delay, port congestion that holds up haulage, or a misinterpreted contract, and put them in front of the operator early enough for them to act. Command Center surfaces the risks, the AI agents take routine tracking and reconciling off the operator’s plate, and Freight Audit checks carrier invoices against the contract and the actual shipment, so overcharges and miscalculated D&D are caught before they are paid rather than written off after. BCOs are already benchmarking their forwarders on exactly that, and it is often the difference between an account that renews and one that goes out to tender. For most forwarders, the honest answer is uncomfortable, and it is also the easiest money they will find all year.

Singapore, Geneva and Houston will remain its main trading centres, with chairman and chief executive Gary Pedersen based in Houston. The December transaction left the company fully owned by senior employees and brought Pedersen into the chief executive role. Centalion said the legal entity will continue through the redomiciliation process, while existing contracts and commercial obligations will remain unaffected. The new brand took effect on October 2 and will be rolled out across the group over the coming months. The group has had a Singapore presence since 2006 and is one of the world’s largest privately held commodity traders. It moved 253m tonnes of commodities last year, including around 3.3m barrels per day of liquids, generating $144bn in revenue and ending 2025 with $6.1bn of equity. The founder’s departure followed renewed scrutiny of the trader’s historical Russia links and a US-blocked attempt to acquire international assets from sanctioned Russian oil major Lukoil.

items.original_title: Neptune Bunker Information Update: Off-Spec Trends Highlight Risk Areas
items.summary: The Neptune Bunker Information tab has been updated with bunker quality data covering April to September 2026, providing Members with further insight into regional fuel quality trends and areas of elevated risk. Several ports record high levels of technical off-specification results across the residual and low-sulphur fuel sectors. Among HFO samples, the highest technical off-specs were recorded in Antwerp (46.2%), Norfolk (41.4%), Panama Canal (38.0%), and Rotterdam (35.5%). Rotterdam samples recorded a sulphur off-spec rate of 68.6%, while samples in Antwerp reached 58.9%, the highest levels seen in the current dataset. Although the number of samples involved is substantially smaller than in other major bunkering ports, the results underline the importance of maintaining robust bunker procurement, testing and fuel management procedures, particularly in respect of emission control regulatory requirements. Within the ULSFO category, the highest technical off-spec percentages were reported in Barcelona (70.3%) and Genoa (51.0%). In both ports, the results were primarily associated with pour point non-compliances, highlighting the need for careful consideration of storage and handling requirements, particularly where low ambient temperatures may become operationally significant. Members are encouraged to continue following established bunker testing and fuel management practices and to make use of Neptune’s fuel quality intelligence when evaluating supply risks and preparing bunkering plans. items.original_title: Russia could partially open diesel exports in case of surplus output: Novak
items.summary: Russia could consider partially opening diesel exports once it returns to a production surplus, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told its Federation Council Oct. 2, describing the market as balanced and sufficiently supplied, local media reported. Traditionally the world’s number-two diesel exporter, Russia started shutting in its diesel production in July following persistent Ukrainian drone attacks on its refining sector, now extended until the end of October. For non-producers, which include traders and refineries with capacities of less than 1 million metric tons/year, the ban will remain in place until the end of January. The deputy prime minister added that given Russia produces more diesel than it consumes, it is necessary to avoid accumulating more stocks than the country has the capacity to store, which would force refineries to reduce throughput and affect the output of other products. Novak’s comments come a day after Russia’s President Vladimir Putin said at the Valday Forum in Moscow that Russia had sufficient diesel but warned the fuel wouldn’t make it to international markets because of foreign sanctions. Gasoline was the first type of fuel export banned by the Kremlin back in April, and the restriction has since been extended through to the end of January 2027.

items.summary: Japan’s Namura Shipbuilding is absorbing its wholly owned Imari Steel Center as the shipbuilder moves to tighten control of production ahead of a major expansion of its newbuilding business. The Osaka-listed builder has approved the merger, with the transaction scheduled to take effect on April 1, 2027. Namura will remain the surviving company and Imari Steel Center will be dissolved. Imari Steel Center sits next to Namura’s main Imari yard in Saga prefecture and handles the upstream steel functions supporting vessel construction, including unloading, sorting, storage, processing and quality assurance of shipbuilding plate. Namura said combining the operations should speed up decision-making, allow better deployment of personnel and other resources, improve manufacturing efficiency and help with recruitment and training as the group increases newbuilding output. The internal reshuffle comes as Namura embarks on one of its biggest capacity pushes in years. Japan’s transport ministry last month approved up to ¥49.9bn ($319m) of government backing for an investment programme involving Namura and subsidiary Hakodate Dock, part of Tokyo’s wider drive to rebuild domestic shipbuilding capacity. Namura is also moving ahead with a new large construction dock, the first major shipbuilding dock to be developed in Japan since Imabari Shipbuilding completed its Marugame facility in 2017.

The buyer vehicle is Norway’s Anchor Australia, set to be folded into the rapidly growing AHTS platform backed by 2020 Bulkers. The deal comes after Akastor’s first attempt to dispose of the vessel fell through last year. DDW agreed a $25m sale of the ship in March 2025, but the transaction was cancelled after the charterer declined to approve novation of the contract. DDW has steadily emptied its AHTS fleet since then. items.title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.original_title: What Is the Shadow Fleet, and Why Is It So Hard to Count?
items.summary: There Is No Official Shadow Fleet List The shadow fleet, also called the dark fleet, refers to tankers and support vessels that rely on deceptive shipping practices to move sanctioned or high-risk commodities while concealing their true origin, ownership, or destination. It has no standing in law, and that is where the difficulty starts. Why Every Published Estimate Is Different Ask five organizations how large the shadow fleet is, and you will get five answers, sometimes differing by a factor of three. The useful question is narrower: Does this vessel exhibit the behavior, and what is my exposure if it does? A vessel flying a legitimate flag has the right of innocent passage through the territorial sea, and on the high seas it is subject to the jurisdiction of its flag state. There is a lag between a vessel starting to operate as part of the shadow fleet and that vessel appearing on a sanctions list. During that gap, the vessel is detectable through its behavior and invisible to a list check. Vessels without a valid flag are stateless, and under Article 110 of UNCLOS, a warship may board a ship on the high seas where there are reasonable grounds to suspect it is.

items.title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
items.original_title: Strait of Hormuz security, decarbonisation among key issues discussed by BIMCO committees
items.summary: The security situation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Black and Red Seas, as well as environmental topics, were among the key issues discussed when BIMCO’s Maritime Safety & Security Committee (MSSC) and Marine Environment Committee (MEC) met on 30 September and 1 October. Members considered the implications of regional conflicts, attacks on shipping, drones, mines and navigational disruption. The committees also discussed a broad range of other regulatory, safety and environmental issues affecting the day-to-day operation of ships. Our committees bring together industry expertise to identify practical challenges and help shape BIMCO’s positions in discussions with the IMO, governments and regulators. Digitalisation was another major theme, including the opportunities it offers for efficiency, compliance and safety, as well as the growing importance of cyber security and supporting seafarers as technology develops. Members also discussed the safe adoption of alternative fuels, including ammonia, hydrogen and methanol, and future safety frameworks for advanced modular nuclear reactors. The proposed legally-binding international convention on biofouling was also discussed, with an emphasis on ensuring that future requirements are practical, science-based and capable of consistent implementation across the global fleet. Other topics included search and rescue and mixed migration, underwater radiated noise, marine plastics and plastic pellet transportation, and implementation of the Hong Kong Convention on ship recycling. Source: BIMCO, https://www.bimco.org/news-insights/bimco-news/2026/10/01-mec-mssc/

items.title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.original_title: Clean tanker markets size up impact of potential US diesel export curbs
items.summary: US restrictions on diesel exports would upend Atlantic Basin clean tanker demand at a moment when the global middle-distillate market is reeling from simultaneous supply shocks in Russia and the Middle East, BRS Shipbrokers said in a report. The impact on medium-range tanker earnings in particular could be swift and severe, BRS said Sept. 28. US President Donald Trump had floated a diesel export ban in response to record domestic fuel prices ahead of midterm elections. Tanker implications A full ban could strand around 1.35 million b/d of US Gulf diesel exports — the equivalent of four MR2-sized cargoes per day — with Europe and Latin America most exposed given the absence of readily available alternative supply, BRS said. Pressure would fall most heavily on MR2s, which carry more than 90% of US diesel exports, BRS said. There could also be bleed-in to MR1 markets as MR2s compete for smaller stems, while clean tankers would likely ballast away from the US Gulf, putting pressure on tonnage lists elsewhere, BRS said. The offsetting factor for the broader clean tanker complex is a potential redirection of Asian barrels westward. “With the potential diesel ban coming, the appetite for US diesel exports is declining because these products are needed at home, whether there’s a ban or not,” Simpson said.

items.original_title: Electric and hybrid ferries could cut emissions by 63% in Sea of Marmara, IMO study finds
items.summary: Türkiye’s Sea of Marmara ferry network could cut greenhouse gas emissions by 63% by switching to a mix of hybrid and fully electric vessels, while avoiding nearly half a billion euros in health and environmental damage costs and supporting around 1,100 jobs a year, according to a new IMO study. Commissioned by IMO’s GreenVoyage2050 programme in partnership with Türkiye’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure, the study assessed 67 Ro-Ro and Ro-Pax ferries carrying vehicles and passengers across 26 ports. The network transports around 25 million passengers and seven million vehicles each year. Significant potential to cut emissions The study found that battery-electric and hybrid propulsion are technically feasible options across all Ro-Pax and Ro-Ro ferry operations assessed in the Sea of Marmara. It identified an optimum scenario combining hybrid and fully electric vessels to balance emissions reductions and costs. Under this scenario, annual GHG emissions could fall by around 63% by 2050 compared with business-as-usual operations using diesel fuel. The transition would also reduce local air pollution and could avoid an estimated €492 million in cumulative health and environmental damage costs. Going further, converting the entire fleet to fully electric operations could cut GHG emissions by 84% by 2050.

UK Maritime Trade Operations, which did not name the vessel, said it received a third-party report that a tanker had been hit, triggering a fire onboard. Maritime security sources identified them as ADNOC-operated VLCC Mersin Prosperity , the 115,949 dwt Sinbad and product tanker Al Ruwais . The pipeline restarted on September 22 and tanker loading resumed several days later, with crude exports from Yanbu estimated at about 2m barrels per day. Cabinet has also approved a feasibility study into bringing in a minority equity partner from one of South Africa’s development finance institutions. South Africa’s ports have endured a prolonged period of congestion, equipment shortages, inadequate maintenance and declining productivity. Durban plunged back into heavy congestion in August, with vessels facing waits of eight to 12 days and some carriers reporting delays of up to 20 days following disruption around the terminal’s operating-system change. Private capital is increasingly central to Pretoria’s attempted ports revival. ICTSI began operating Durban’s flagship Pier 2 terminal this year under a 25-year partnership involving around R11bn ($638m) of investment after a lengthy legal battle delayed the concession. TNPA has also launched private-sector processes covering Cape Town’s multipurpose terminal, a new floating drydock there and the Richards Bay dry bulk terminal, while Transnet last week opened the qualification process for a private partner for the R30bn-R44bn Ngqura manganese corridor.

items.title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.original_title: Suez Transits Are Up 59%, and Rates Are About to Fall
items.summary: Carriers Have Returned to Suez, and the Data Confirms It Maritime media sources state that container shipping is moving from a capacity shortage to a surplus as carriers return to Suez and shorter voyages free up ships. Suez containership transits rose 59% from March to September, from 139 to 221. The growth came from large ships, 300m and above, up to 24,000 TEU, the post-Panamax to ultra-large vessels used on main Asia-Europe services, which rose from 22 to 127 transits a month. Around 100 more large containerships now transit the Suez Canal instead of around Africa, compared to March, cutting one to two weeks off each round trip. Suez routing for Asia-Europe services has recovered to only about a quarter of pre-crisis levels, per Sea-Intelligence. Even a partial return matters, because carriers expanded Asia-Europe capacity by approximately 41% between May 2023 and May 2025 to cover the longer route around Africa, according to Alphaliner, meaning that every service that switches back to Suez frees ships the route no longer needs. Shorter voyages mean each liner service needs fewer ships to keep its schedule, freeing capacity just as Europe-bound demand softens after the summer and ahead of China’s Golden Week holiday (1-7 Oct), when factory closures halt much of China’s export production.

items.title: Tankers enter the death zone
items.original_title: Tankers enter the death zone
items.summary: Like climbers entering the death zone above 8,000 metres en route to the summit of Everest, VLCCs have entered their own peak: the moment where prices for secondhand tonnage surpass newbuild prices, and sell signs flash hard. These moments tend to be fleeting and have historically been associated with the hottest stages of shipping cycles. The question is how often the market has reached this altitude before, and how long it can survive there. The previous maximum premium for a five-year-old VLCC over a newbuild was 21% in December 2007. Veson data shows a 15-year-old VLCC overtook the newbuild value for the first time on September 27. Danish Ship Finance takes a broader approach, using a monthly secondhand-to-newbuilding price ratio for tankers stretching back to January 2000. Its series identifies 11 distinct episodes, including the current one. “To stay with your analogy: the death zone usually punishes those who linger — but in 2003–08, the market camped up there for nearly six years,” Danish Ship Finance told Splash. The completed episodes have averaged around 12 months, although that number is heavily distorted by the extraordinary 2003-08 supercycle, which accounts for more than half of all the months its tanker index has spent above parity.

items.title: BofA raises long-term copper forecast to $12,000 per ton
items.original_title: BofA raises long-term copper forecast to $12,000 per ton
items.summary: Bank of America strategists raised their long-term copper price forecast by 20% to $12,000 per ton, or $5.44 per pound in 2026 dollars, according to a commodities update report. The bank cited ongoing supply issues as the main driver behind copper’s continued price strength. The forecast adjustment comes after more than 12 months of policy and other market surprises, with risks of volatility from war in the Middle East continuing to persist. Bank of America strategists noted potential risks including a possible energy-induced demand shock or a pause in data center capital expenditures. The bank made minimal other changes to its commodity forecasts. It lowered its 2027 aluminum price forecast by 5% to $3,625 per ton. Bank of America said higher interest rates and a stronger dollar create a bearish outlook for gold prices. Source: Investing.com

items.title: India reduces windfall taxes on diesel and jet fuel exports
items.original_title: India reduces windfall taxes on diesel and jet fuel exports
items.summary: India lowered windfall taxes on diesel and aviation turbine fuel exports starting October 1, according to a government order released today. The export duty on diesel fell to 16 rupees per litre from 20 rupees per litre. The levy on aviation turbine fuel exports dropped to 10.5 rupees per litre from 15 rupees per litre. The export duty on petroleum products remained at 0.5 rupees per litre. Source: Investing.com
